Question: How can I die? I have lost my love and I am alone.
Answer: I was in the surgical emergency room. It was a very heavy shift and me being an intern was busy running around following everyone's orders. At around 2 AM came in a patient. He came on a stretcher, unconscious, head was bleeding, limbs broken. His left tibia and fibula (shin bones) were broken and protruding from the skin. It was one of the worst cases I had seen till then in my short medical life. He was a 24 year old boy who jumped from a multi storey building because his girlfriend broke up with him. There was a slim to none chance of him surviving, yet my seniors followed the protocol, trying to save him. He didn't make it. What happened after that? Who was crying in the emergency room? His ex? No buddy, it was his parents. The middle aged couple arrived shortly after the ambulance. As soon as they saw his state, I could see them turning around in a fraction of a second. They just could not see their young son with bones protruding. In the few minutes that he was still alive, his mother was praying to the small Ganpati idol we had in there. As they were standing there, I heard his father say to his mother, “Don't worry, I am there na. Why are you getting scared? I will handle everything. I'll not let him die”. Imagine a 55–60year old man, giving false hopes to his wife about things he had zero control over. You know what was worse? He was crying just as hard while reassuring her. I have seen death, but I had never seen a family die. It wasn't just the guy who died, his parents lost their souls too. I cannot describe her scream. I cannot describe how I saw two souls crumble before me. The moment they knew he was no more, their world was over. I could already see them spending the rest of their lives trying to figure out where they went wrong, what could they have done to prevent it. Imagine the pain you're feeling that you lost your love. Now multiply it by a million, that's how much pain parents feel when their child kills himself/herself. Nothing, and I mean NOTHING is worth putting your parents through hell. Suicide is a rather selfish act. You become free, but the family you leave behind spends the rest of the life wondering what went wrong. Like it or not, your life isn't just your life, it belongs in bits to everyone who loves you. Most importantly, the only people who really lose their reason to survive are your parents. Heartbreak, failure, financial loss.. everything is but a chapter in your life. As cliché as it may sound, they are but a chapter not the whole book. I know it hurts, I have been through it. It feels like you'll never love again, you'll never forget that person. But you know what? Life moves on. Ever so slowly they become a memory you rarely think about. You start feeling whole again. Irrespective of what the movies tell you, the heart heals itself. The scars fade away and you're ready to love again. 'You only fall in love once' is bulls**t. You just learn from the past and make better choices till you meet your one and only! If it didn't last it just wasn't meant to be. You'll get a new love. And even if you don't, the pain is going to ease. It’s very naive to think this is the end of it all. Next time you think about ending your life over something as temporary, just call your parents. And imagine that voice without a soul. Is anything worth losing that? Absolutely not. Next time, take a pause, live for just one more day. I can assure you, that one day will change your mind.

Question: How do doctors handle patient complaints and how does it impact their relationship with the patient?
Answer: I think every doctor faces this sometime or the other. Medicine is a high stakes field. Every single thing we do affects the patients so intimately, even a small mistake can be a cause of a lot anguish and complaints (often rightfully so). I often say to my non-medico husband, when you make mistakes your company might lose some money but when I make mistakes, people die. So, once you understand this concept, a doctor can become more empathetic towards patient’s complaints. Initially, I used to get very worked up with even the smallest of complaints by the patients. I used to rack my brains, thinking how could I go wrong. But as time has passed, I have realised the key to actually solve the problem is to not take it personally. Patients are usually already worried with their illnesses, so their complaints have a lot to do with their general state of distress. So just be, empathetic. Understand where the dissatisfaction is coming from. And if you see any mistakes from your side, just come forth with 100% honesty. In my experience, this approach usually works. Patients appreciate an honest and truthful dialogue. So just accept your mistake, remedy it and don’t repeat it the next time. You’ll gain that patient’s trust for life. As for me, even if the patient complains; it absolutely does not affect my relationship with them. I don’t believe doctors are above mistakes and consequences. We are human, we can make mistakes and when we do, people have the right to complaint. I do, however, have zero tolerance policy towards violence. So if a patient starts getting aggressive with his complaints, I usually refer them to another specialist.

Question: As a surgeon, have you opened somebody up only to realise that they were beyond saving?
Answer: Unfortunately, yes. There was this patient, 55 year old guy. He came with acute abdominal pain. The patient was in severe distress and the vitals weren’t good even at presentation. He was way too unstable to get a CT scan so we went ahead with just an Ultrasound. Ultrasound wasn’t very conclusive but it suggested intestinal obstruction. The patient was just getting worse and worse so we gave him initial resuscitation and decided to open him. We were prepared to face unexpected scenarios. But we weren’t prepared for what it actually was. As soon as we entered the abdominal cavity, copious amounts of reddish liquid oozed out. A little deeper and there it was..about 80% of his stomach, duodenum, the entire small intestine a portion of ascending and transverse colon were almost black in colour. Every surgeon’s arch nemesis…Superior Mesentric Artery thrombosis. But in this case Stomach was also involved. Basically, the blood supply to his stomach and his entire small intestine and parts of large intestine was compromised. Due to this the parts were ischaemic. There is nothing you can do in this situation. If there was enough healthy gut remaining we would have just cut out the dead part and anastomosed the healthy parts. There just wasn’t enough healthy gut here. So we just closed the patient up, informed the relatives and sent the patient back to the ICU where he passed away a few hours later, surrounded by his family. It’s very disheartening for a surgeon to accept there’s nothing you can do for the patient in front of you. But then, a good surgeon knows when to cut but the best ones know when not to. Just operating when we knew he wouldn’t survive the procedure would have led to him dying on the table. Atleast by closing him up he could pass away surrounded by his family. And believe me, that matters. That matters to the patient and that matters to the family. And while I was heartbroken at losing my patient, it gave me the tiniest bit of satisfaction knowing that we could give that family the last few hours with him. And, hopefully, we could give them closure. P.S. So, a lot of you are interested in the risk factors and how to diagnose the condition. Here’s an article that explains SMA thrombosis is simple terms by Eduardo Franca; Maxim E. Shaydakov; Jason Kosove.

Question: What are some morning habits that can change your day?
Answer: Well begun is half done! Mornings can give you the perfect kickstart for your day when done right. But, a crappy morning can just start the day off wrong, right?! Like a spilled tea, a missed bus, broken heel… and there goes your day! These are a few things that work for me to start off my mornings well 1. When you wake up, just get up- There was an article I read a few years back that talked about this term called, ‘Horizontal depression’. It mentioned how when you are just laying down in bed and thinking negative thoughts, all those negatives just get magnified. When you get up and face the day, you feel like you’re in charge and just feel better. A little better. As a doctor , I can’t give any medical reasoning for this, but as a patient I can tell you that I have personally experienced this to be really effective when I had my bouts of depression. So when you get up in the morning, don’t just lazy around. Just get up, take charge and seize the day! Carpe diem! 2. Make your bed- This is something I find to be very very helpful and make a point to do everyday. See this simple act of making your bed means so much. You’re starting the day with accomplishing a task, you’re organising your space, you’re keeping your bed ready for the next night! So many goals with one simple task! It really energises your space and that energises you! 3. A tall glass of water- I like to have a glass of water in the morning. I tried warm water, but couldn’t! So room temp water it is! But it’s just so refreshing. Helps that with 7–8 hours of thirst and a good way to wake your gut up. 4. Have a screen free morning- Well we’re all guilty of losing track of time as we lay doom scrolling on the phone. But that’s just not productive. You lose valuable morning minutes (sometimes hours!) and achieve nothing. Reading a few silly WhatsApp forwards, watching edited reels on instagram or reading a ton on bad news on Twitter isn’t going to help you get going for the day. Keep all that aside for later, focus on your day, focus on yourself. 5. Have a schedule/to-do-list- I always like to have a to-do-list for the day. Even a rough timeline is fine. But it keeps you on track. Being able to check things off is an added plus! This is the my to-do-list notepad. It’s simple, effective and gives me a little giggle every morning! 6. Dress up for the day- For me, this is the one thing that makes me feel my best. To dress up for the day. Even if I don’t plan to leave to my house, I like to dress up a little every morning. Just a fresh tshirt and jeans can elevate your day. Pyjamas are comfy and I would live in them if I could, but they are not the push you need for an awesome day! Just go that little extra mile and dress up for the day. And a swipe of lip balm never hurt nobody! Some mornings you might not want to leave your bed, but you just have to. Monday mornings are the usual culprits. So just GET UP, DRESS UP AND SHOW UP. Today might just be the day that’ll change your life!

Question: What is it that you find most attractive about people?
Answer: Kindness. I think kindness is the most important value that attracts me to people. It is the single most underrated virtue. But so, so essential. You can have all the smarts, money, good looks but if you don’t have kindness, what use is any of the above. How you treat others, how you make others feel, that’s what really matters in the end. As I grow older, a lot of things that felt important at some point have started losing their charm. The best looking guy may be a jerk to the waiter, the girl in the BMW might just kick a puppy, the guy with a Harvard degree may be a bully. Of course material things are exciting and fun, but if you are not kind, you cannot form a genuine bond with anyone. How you treat others matters. How you make others feel matters. We need to start adding “people” in our lives and not portfolios. At the end of the day, after all the spotlights dim, people are only going to remember how you made them feel. So ask yourself…. Are you kind to the stranger on the street? Are you kind to your friends and family? Are you kind to yourself?

Question: Why do you think most relationships fail?
Answer: Good relationships are not built by being together in good times, the ones that last are the ones where people stick together in the bad times. For me, that is why relationships fail. When we get into relationships, we forget that it’s not all sunshine and rainbows. There are going to be bad times because Hello! Welcome to the real world. But bad times by themselves don’t mean a bad relationship. We need to not give up in the bad times. We need to especially stick together in the bad times. Often, we take the easy way out. Because giving up is just way easier. What is not easy is sitting together and talking about the unpleasant, finding a solution no matter how messy, helping the other person get back on their feet, catching your partner from falling because we all slip up sometimes! If you can help each other in bad times, you’re going to get your forever! Don’t give up on your love because things get tough. Stay together, fight together, help each other out. Sometimes you’ll be the one needing help too and you’re going to want your partner to be their for you too! Most relationships fail because they give each other good times but give up in the bad times! Don’t give up on each other! Remember why you love your person!

Question: What was the hardest lesson you learned from your first romantic relationship?
Answer: My first relationship was with my ex. I have written about it before. To say it was difficult is an understatement. I wasted quite a few years of my life in that relationship. At the end of it, things got so bad that I went into clinical depression and had to put in everything I had to bring my life back on track. While I was really broken by the relationship, the hardest lesson I learnt has to be “LOVE IS SIMPLY NOT ENOUGH” Yes, you read that right. And no I’m not materialistic. I was in my early 20s and hadn’t seen much of the world. My idea of love came from Bollywood movies and Jane Austen novels. I believed love is hard, or rather it has to be hard. That if you love each other, all other fights and hurts are ok. But now I know better. Love simply isn’t enough. You need to be good to and for each other. You need to have respect for each other. There has to be a friendship. You should be able to work together as a team. You need to not hurt each other. Shahrukh swaying his arms with his dimpled smile maybe enough in a movie, but in real life, he needs to be able to come home and make you laugh and help you do the dishes!

Question: What is everyone doing during the coronavirus?
Answer: Well I am doing what I did before…working! I am a surgery resident, life is pretty much the same in this pandemic. Wake up, go to the hospital, OPD, surgeries, emergency calls..the works! There have been a few significant changes though. We have reduced the number of elective procedures. We pretty much only do emergency surgeries these days. Since corona virus in present in a large concentration in the peritoneal fluid, we wear full protective gear in OT as well. So that's a really hot, uncomfortable 2–3 surgery! We wear basic PPE even in the OPD now. So no more cute clothes, same old scrubs with mask and cap and face shield! It's very suffocating to say the least, but hey, protection above everything else. This is me in OPD today There have been changes in my post hospital schedule though. As soon as I get home, I go directly for a hot water shower. I don't enter through the main door. My bag, shoes, powerbank, lunch box all are kept outside the house and santized. I keep them there till the next morning till I pack again. After shower, I go directly in my room where I have my dinner and stay in my room till the next day. I don't spend time face to face with my parents, I don't let my niece hug me. After being around so many patients all day, I can never be sure that I am corona free! I cannot risk spreading it. Next day starts the same cycle all over again. That's what my life is during this period.. surrounded by everyone, yet lonely. Living in constant fear.

Question: What does depression look like?
Answer: What does it look like? A sad, teary eyed girl sitting in a filthy room with papers scattered around the room and a half eaten pizza? Or an unkept young man, overgrown beard surrounded by empty beer cans and cigarette butts? Ha! If only it was that simple. Depression is also that girl who always keeps smiling, that boy who keeps cracking jokes. That doctor who drives a Ferrari. Or that actress who just won an Oscar. Depression looks like all of the above. We ofter relate depression with the simplistic outwardly sad appearance we see in the movies. But appearances are Often deceiving. Which is why we often miss the obvious depression in people all around us. We need to start actually seeing people than just looking at them. We need to see beyond the smiles. We need to listen more. Sometimes a loud laugh is just a cry for help. This is me in my worst phases of depression, at Disneyland, the happiest place on earth! Ironic, isn't it? This is me today, after a very long work day, in dull old hospital scrubs. Well kept? Naa. Happy? You bet! My point is, depression doesn't look like a textbook presentation. Sure, many patients will fit that bill. But many won't. And we need to be aware of that.

Question: As a physician, how does your relationship with a patient (BOTH professional and non-professional) affect your ability to offer an objective opinion?
Answer: A2A This is a dilema, for physicians in general but especially for me. Ever since my first day of med school. I have actually written an article about the same in my college magazine! Short answer, having a relationship with a patient isn't going to help my ability as a physician. I'll be more careful, sure, but I'll also doubt myself way more. And there's nothing worse than doubting yourself. Once doubt sets in, efficiency goes down. So, personally, I would strongly advice against treating someone you care about. Long answer- This query arises because our profession deals with real people with real lives. Everything that we do, every word we say has a very direct impact on the person in front of us and his/her own family. As far as treating someone you have a non professional (personal) relationship with goes, I don't think it's ever a good idea. No matter how hard you try, your ability to give an opinion or treat is going to clouded by your feelings towards the patient. We are humans after all, heart always find a way to over power the brain. Our views will be affected. It's like Dr. Astana says in Munnabhai MBBS, your hand is gonna shake while operating your kid. You'll look for reasons to not believe a bad prognosis, you'll either over treat or under. And none of it is in the best interest of the patient. No matter how hard you try, you simply cannot put your feelings aside. So if it's someone you have a personal relationship with, i would rather stay a friend than a physician. Because I, personally cannot put my feelings aside enough to be a good doctor for them. Now here's a catch though, (and not directly related to your question!) I would still rather build a professional relationship with a patient I am treating than be completely, emotionally shut off. I like asking patients about their lives, if they are happy, I like listening to their stories. It helps me connect, I can be more aware of their needs. It helps build a rapport that's ultimately going to help both of us. Medicine is rarely 2+2 = 4. It's often 3/5. What makes it 3 or 5? The patient. To know the disease, you have to know the patient. It's about finding that fine balance where you build a relationship with your patients just enough to think of them as a person not patient but not so much that you think then as a friend and not a person! See there was sign outside my internal medicine department, “A good doctor treats patients, a great doctor treats people!”

Question: What's the hardest truth of life?
Answer: Death. Death is the hardest and ultimate truth of life. You can go round and round, sugarcoat it, pretend like you've any control over it but there it remains…the ultimate truth. I am a doctor, I've probably faced death more than other people. But, the realisation of the inevitability of death dawned to me after I lost my beloved grandmother. My aaji, my dad's mom. She was very very close to me. Since my mom is a working woman, my aaji had a lion's share in raising me. She was my mom. All my childhood memories are with her. She was so so proud of me. Even though she was 89, I just never thought she'll actually leave us all. Silly, I know. Naive, for sure. But, when it comes to people you love, do you actually ever want to believe they are not going to be with you forever? Her death was a massive shock to me, it's been 6 months and I still can't get over it. The idea that I will never hear her call me 'baudi' makes me heartbroken. The fact that I may one day forget her voice crushes me. When my grandmother was sick, I kind of downplayed it. I had that arrogance that she'll fight it all, we'll fight it all. My dad's a doctor, so am I and most of our friends. Aaji was so strong, one illness can't do her any harm. But when that unfortunate moment came, none of us could do anything. We just had to see her go. There was no rhyme or reason. There was no coming back from there. As much as I miss her every moment, nothing anyone can do can bring her back. And every single life has to face death, some sooner, some later. But it's inevitable. It's that inevitability of death that makes life so precious. That's where it ends. Life ends in the ultimate truth.. death.

Though he is working from home, his roommate still has to go to work. I keep warning him about taking precautions and I just hope he is telling the truth when he says he's being careful, my sister is working from home and my niece and nephew have started home schooling. My husband's working from home and I know he's being very cautious. I am upset that I won't be meeting him in June, because I am pretty sure this isn't gonna be ok till then. Question: As a doctor, have you ever broken down into tears while explaining a prognosis or diagnosis to a patient?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. This is not an easy situation to be in. I've been there. So there was this patient, a 24 year old girl who came with her parents for bleeding per rectum, after initial assessment we thought it to be thrmobosed haemorrhoids. So we told her parents it's a pretty routine surgery and all. On the day of surgery, she was very very anxious. She asked me to hold her hand through the surgery and I did. I asked out of assisting the procedure and stood there, holding her hand. And as the anesthesia set in, and the procedure started we discovered it wasn't just haemorrhoids, it was rectal cancer. We took a biopsy and stopped the procedure. After the procedure, we had to explain to the family. We requested for an urgent pet scan the same day. The cancer had already metastasized to her liver and other parts. My professor gave her an year max We had to explain to the parents of a 24 year old, unmarried girl that their daughter had Stage 4 carcinoma. We had to explain to them that there wasn't much we, or any doctor for that matter, could do at that point. The same daughter that I held hands with a day before. How do you do that without breaking down? How do you put on a straight face? You just do. You tell the news without betraying an iota of emotion, then you wait for the door to close and it is then that you break down. You break down and cry till you run out of tears. Then you come out of the room and move on to the next patient. Because that's what you're supposed to do. When you have that white coat on, you're a doctor. When you remove it, that's when you're allowed to be human.

Question: Does anyone want to write their heart out here?

What happens when things go wrong? How do you get back to work the next day when you wake up feeling like a murderer? You just do. You get humbled by the realisation that at the end of the day, you're not God. Then you get ready, put on that white coat, and march ahead. Head held high, heart just a little bit broken.

Question: Is Bakson's Vitamin D+ capsules safe to take everyday?
Answer: A2A Note- not to be substituted for proffesional advice. Vit D is a fat soluble vitamin (unlike vit B and C which are water soluble). Hence excess amounts cannot be washed off in urine and can cause side effects. Question: What does being depressed feel like?
Answer: You ever wondered how the witches and wizards in Harry Potter felt after the dementors sucked their souls away? That is what depression feels like. Actually that is exactly what depression feels like. Apparently, J. K. Rowling wrote about dementors based on her own experience with depression. 6.10 AM I wake up every morning at 6.10 AM, no alarm, no purpose. I wake with palpitations, sweating. Feeling doomed. Every single thing I ever did wrong, comes right back at me. I scroll through the phone, BuzzFeed or twitter or Quora. Not registering anything, still reading everything. I then put on some random YouTube video till my mind is numb enough to fall back to sleep. And I do. 7.30 AM This is when I am actually supposed to get up, but I can't. The alarm rings, I hear it and try to ignore. Till I cannot. Then I hit the snooze again and again. I am not even actually sleepy, I just don't see the point in getting up. Same day, same anxiety, same regrets. Atleast the bed doesn't remind me of my own failures. Then when even the bed becomes uncomfortable, I get up and get ready. 8.30 AM Yoga. This part is good… sometimes. On the good days, that one hour rejuvenates me for the entire day. Helps me not break down. On the bad days, it's hard to focus for even one meditation or excercise. Everytime I close my eyes, I am reminded of something that's wrong with my life. Every exercise seems pointless, because how can anything solve my messed up life? I leave the class feeling sadder than before. Because it is just another failure. 10.30/11.30/12.30/never I'm supposed to come go to the library and study. Exam is barely a month away. I get ready, put some makeup on, hoping external beauty would somehow transfer on the inside. LoL! As I keep telling myself how crucial it is to keep going, it makes more anxious. I keep delaying stepping out my room. The tiny four walled safe space, where I know I'm not letting anyone down. Somedays I make it out of the house, sometimes I just stay in. Doing nothing, feeling guilty about doing nothing. Sometime during the day I eat, because that's just something I can do. I talk to people (if I can), not really registrating what the talk is about. I smile, it never reaches your eyes. 11 PM/ 12 PM/ 1 AM/ never I get into bed. Something I keep longing for all day and keep dreading at the time. The room which seems like my safe space during the day, somehow turns into a monster at night. The bed seems alien. I feel tired and exhausted but too restless to sleep. Every single thing wrong with life, comes back. Flashbacks of my mistakes, friends I hurt, opportunities I lost, whats and ifs, could've and should've. All right there, naked, for me ponder over in the depths of darkness. The clock keeps ticking, thoughts keep getting darker. I put some makeup tutorial on YouTube, their fixed, purposeful actions seem soothing. After a few videos I fall asleep. Headphones still in place. The routine repeats. And repeats. And repeats. When I was young er , I always imagined depressed people to look very unkept, crying all the time, sleeping in bed all day everyday. Oh how I was mistaken. Most of is suffering from depression don't look a any different than anyone else. Infact, I am more well dressed than most because that helps in pretending to be happy and normal. It feels like you're in a glass box. You can see all the bright colours and happiness outside. But it appears just a little dull to you, there's a film on your eyes. You can see all the happiness outside but the glass doesn't let you reach it. It also doesn't let anyone hear when you shout out. When you cry, cry because you're broken and then cry some more because you don't get the reason. You feel a heavy weight on your chest and you cannot move no matter how hard you try Apathy. That's what you feel, or don't feel. Smiles are not joyous, tears are not sorrowful. Everyday is a struggle between your mind trying to make you give up on life, and your brain trying to make you see the selfishness behind that thought. What keeps me going? Knowing that things are going to change. Someday. Even on the worst day, you make it through. This time is going to move on, you're going to make it through this. This is a line from a poem I loved, it's on YouTube

Question: What have you tried for 30 days that changed everything?
Answer: Yoga and meditation! This might sound very cliché but yoga has single handedly helped me survive the last few months. I have mentioned in a previous answer about a panic attack that made me lose an opportunity of a lifetime. I lost a seat in an excellent institute just because I couldn't stay in the room any longer and had to, literally, run away from there. The realisation of what I've lost hit me the moment my plane landed in my city. I cried from the moment I sat in the car to the next few weeks. It wasn't the cute, silent cry. It was the howling, shouting cry. I spend days and weeks regretting my decision. Hoping I can somehow get it back. Day and night didn't make any sense. Neither did food or water. Waking up didn't make sense. It was like my entire life seemed had become one gloomy cloud. The only thing that stopped me from doing something drastic was my niece and my parents. I lived for them. Then one day my mom took me to her yoga class. I went with a very clear plan of dropping it the next day. But she paid my 3 month fees on day one so I had to continue! I went on the first day, then second and then continued for the next 30 days. And God!! I cannot even describe how it changed my mind, my soul, my life. I got up every morning, got dressed, cleaned my room and went to yoga. That 1 hour became the favourite part of my day. All the dull, depressing thoughts were gone. Things seems happier, more hopeful. I started studying again, with more vigour. There was like a surge of energy in me. My sleep cycle became more regular than it had been in years. Gone were the feelings of regret, guilt, loss. There was only hope, only happiness. Ofcourse, this didn't solve my problems completely. But it did give me the power to solve them. Yoga and meditation helps you focus. It centers your mind in a way that you can really apply yourself to whatever you decide to. Apart from the physical benefits, what it does for your mind is priceless. That 1 month of regular Yoga has hooked me on for life! I even suggested this to my friend who was suffering from depression. Even she benefitted immensely from it. So if any of you are going through depression or anxiety, you should definitely give yoga a try (though it's in no way an alternative to medicines but rather a supplement to them.) Whatever success I'll get this year, it'll be due to this 1 month!

Question: Have you ever mistakenly received a text you weren’t supposed to get?
Answer: Well my mistaken text also happens to be one of the most bizarre things I have ever experienced! A few years back, when I was in 2nd year I got a text on my phone, “Hi Pooja, can you please pick up the phone? Everyone is saying you got married but I refuse to believe. I will die if I don't get a reply.” Now my name isn't Pooja (duh!), neither was my roommate's. Someone (let's calling him A) had sent it mistakenly. At first I thought someone is pranking me. But I had just gotten that number, so it could just have been the previous owner's name. I told that person this isn't Pooja and he has texted the wrong number. And then the interesting part began. He called. I didn't pick up because I usually reject unknown numbers. But then he kept calling and calling and calling. I had 28 missed calls from him. And then a new number (let's call him B) started calling. I picked up. B was A's brother. What he told next was heart breaking. B told me, Pooja was A's girlfriend. And she indeed had my number before me. They were in a long distance relationship. Pooja had an accident and lost her life a few days back. And since A's family thought it'll be too hard for him to digest they told him she got married and hence won't talk to him. He asked me if I can chat with A, pretending to be Pooja for a few days till he believes she is actually married. I was shocked. I didn't know if I could believe him. And honestly, I didn't need to get in the mess...patho, micro, pharma were killing me as is! But B was pleading too much and sounded desperate so I gave in. I chatted with him, pretending to be his ex for a few days, till his family broke the unfortunate news. The whole texting with him thing was super weird. I felt guilty but he seemed over emotional and I understood why his family was so cautious. We chatted for a few days till he seemed to accept Pooja won't be in his life anymore. Then his brother called me again to inform that they are going to tell him the truth. A stopped texting me after that. He called me a week later to apologise and thank. Turned out this bizzare story was actually true. Life is, sometimes, weirder than your imagination! My naive decision to trust a stranger turned out to be a huge help for some unfortunate young man. It may have been morally questionable, but all the hearts were definitely in the right place. We continued to stay in touch over the years. He called me didi! That was one wrong message that I am glad I received. Edit- to everyone commenting this is fake, I take it as a compliment. Also, All said and done, you may believe it or you may not but thank you for reading!

Question: How do I use lavender essential oil to treat an eye infection?
Answer: Well you don't! Essential oils are very concentrated and very potent and should be used with caution. No oil, lavender or otherwise, should be used for eye infection. They should NEVER be in contact with your eyes. Not just oils, but don't put anything in your eyes unless it's prescribed by your ophthalmologist. My father is an ophthalmologist and has seen many cases over the years of people actually losing their eyesight completely or getting permanent damage because of people putting random, non eye safe things in their eyes. Please do not risk your eyesight for 'something you read on the internet'.

Question: What can make my skin glow naturally?
Answer: As someone who struggled for years with acne and horrible dry patches (yup, the lethal combination!) I finally have good skin. Though I still get a few stubborn breakouts here and there, I mostly have a quite plain, glowy skin now. So after trying a million different ways and means for years, these are the things that worked for me. Now I'll get into the natural products that worked for me. African black soap- This soap is traditionally made in Africa with Shea Butter, oat kernels, rosemary, and various leafs and herbs. Though the original form is available online, I prefer a little modified version that is less harsh on the skin from brands like Shea Moisture and Equate beauty. Trust me guys, this soap is MAGIC. Initially it might flare up the acne but on regular use (froth it it up and apply the froth on your face. Wash off with warm water after 2–3 mins) it clears up your skin like nobody's business. It has also significantly reduced my acne marks. I am using this brand these days. But I have also used Shea Moisture and Nubian beauty in the past and all work the same more or less! Essential oils- now this is a very exciting find. I was quite apprehensive about applying oils directly to my face but the right oils can enhance your skin just so much. Some of the combinations that I use are jojoba oil with a few drops of ylang ylang oil, jojoba oil with tea tree, olive oil with lemon oil, olive oil with lavender. Here the first oil acts as a carrier, so use 4–5 drops and the second oil is potent, to be used like a drop or 2. Apply them before sleeping, your skin with be glowy and supple the next morning! This is the brand of essential oils that I have been using. I got them from Amazon and have used up quite a few. Face pack- face pack gives a very deep cleanse to the skin. There are a variety of natural face packs available that suit all the different skin type. But for oily skin, I prefer Aztec clay (available on Amazon), Charcoal masks, the oldie Goldie multani mitti or Fuller's earth. You can take them a little further by adding turmeric, sandalwood powder, aloe vera and apple cider vinegar. Also a simple mask of honey and a few drops of lemon juice can give you that instant glow. So basically, this is how I keep my skin glowy and healthy. It may seem extensive but it's actually quite basic. But maintaining your skin isn't an overnight thing. It takes patience but it's worth it !

Question: What's your recent happiest moment?

You never realise what one kind word from you might mean to someone. My one act of kindness was all that was needed to save a life. The sad part is I wasn't the only one who saw her. There were atleast 10 people who were looking at her without bothering to ask her why she was crying near a railway track. Why is it so hard to be kind? Whoever is reading this just make eye contact, try giving a smile when you see someone in distress. What is a tiny thing for you may be all the assurance someone needs to keep living. Question: What is it like to visit a brothel in India?
Answer: I am going to give you my experience of going to a red light area, but as a doctor. During my internship, we used to have camps in underprivileged areas. One such camp was in Kamathipura, a red light area of Mumbai. Me and a friend were to go there by cab where our senior doctor was going to join us. We were extremely nervous about going there and seeing the patients since neither of us were originally from Mumbai and had no idea what to expect. The first problem was finding a taxi. Imagine two 22 year old girls trying to hail a cab to Kamathipura at 9 AM! Not only was it funny, it was nearly impossible! Taxi drivers refused to take us there for some reason. Then we tried another route, we wore our aprons and stethoscopes! That trick works more often than you might imagine! We finally got in a cab and reached. On the way the driver, who was a very kind old man, warned us to be careful there and all that. We were already nervous, and then we were downright scared! The camp was in a health centre there, we were 3 doctors and 1 pharmacist and the camp started. Whatever apprehensions we had, disappeared immediately. Most patients were the working women, in all age groups. Early twenties to late fifties. Shockingly, most of them had kids. The patients, even though plenty, were very kind. They were polite, empathetic and very patient. There was no rushing and pushing, no fights. They were normal women with kids. Having had my share of aggressive patients, they were a welcome surprise! There was also a very strong sense of attachment between themselves. They were all, in a way, taking care of each other. They had their stories, their concerns, their hopes. They also had many health problems. In the daily struggle of surviving, they had no time or money to look after themselves. So, in short, it was a very humbling experience. And a total opposite of what we expected. It was eye opening. Those women are humans too, trying to survive in a very harsh world. To the world they might be prostitutes; to me, they were just patients.

Question: What are medical students experiences while they were posted in the psychiatry department?
Answer: During my psychiatry rotation, for 2 weeks we had to attend the deaddiction OPD and ward. So one day, the whole batch was following our attending psychiatrist as he went from bed to bed, conducting his routine round and explaining us cases. There was this one patient who was an alcoholic. He was admitted in the deaddiction ward and had not had a drink in 48 hours. As expected, he was in a very aggressive and confused state. His hands and feet were tied down to the bed and he was blabbering. Once our group reached his bed, our attending and rest of my batchemates were standing on the left side of the bed and me and my friend were walking towards the right. That patient, suddenly, pointed towards us and started shouting, “bhaago bhaago bhaise aa rahi hai!” (“Run run, buffaloes are coming towards us!) Our attending asked him where were the buffaloes. He pointed straight at us and said, “Yeh do bhaise nahi dekhi? Meri taraf bhaag rahi hai” (“Can't you see these 2 buffaloes? They're running towards me!”) Oh my God! The whole batch started laughing hysterically! I was so embarrassed! The poor guy was having hallucinations due to alcohol withdrawal. Seeing a herd of cattle is a pretty common hallucination in alcohol withdrawal. But, he did manage to make me insecure about my weight! To be honest, I might have had a roti less for the next few days!

Question: What does a mental breakdown feel like?
Answer: It feels horrible. You feel like a deflated balloon. I have been studying for my PG entrance. It's a highly, highly competitive exam with 1.5 lakh doctors competing for like 15k seats. This year, I had a good score. I had a very good chance of getting a seat of my choice. I literally ran away to the main Street, took a cab and reached the airport 6 hours before my flight. In my mind I knew what a gigantic mistake I am making and yet I couldn't stop myself. It was after the flight landed at my home town and I realised the magnitude of what happened. I have cried for the past 5 days straight. And it isn't that cute silent tears cry, it's an outright ugly, wailing cry. What wouldn't I give to go back there and somehow control my panic attack. In one moment of panic I lost a thing I have worked my ass off for 3 years. So how does a mental breakdown feel like? It feels f**king horrible. You feel so helpless, like you're captive of your own mind. Every rational cell in your body will tell you you're wrong and yet you cannot stop yourself. Like there a fog stopping you from seeing clearly. And it happens to the best of us. I am a doctor, I work as a general practitioner, seeing 80–130 patients daily. I do all that without any glitch. And yet, when the mental breakdown happened, I couldn't help myself. I crushed my dreams, I wandered around in a strange city without thinking of my safety and now I am left with a dead end and tremendous guilt. Why didn't I seek help earlier? I don't have depression or anxiety or any other mental health condition. That's the thing about mental breakdowns, it's as unexpected as it is unpleasant.

Question: Can you give any example of karma in your life?
Answer: I would like to tell the story of my best friend. My best friend is the most amazing, sweetest guy. Very simple, very honest. He was single for the longest time. Then when we were doing internship, he fell for my friend. They eventually started dating, they were in a relationship for 3 years. They continued strong even after college ended and both went to different places for residency. I was very happy for him, as even though they were both completely different somehow he seemed very very happy with her. Then one weekend, he went to visit her to her city. They had a good time, hanging out, meeting her parents and all. After the trip, as he landed at Chennai airport, he called her. She didn't receive. She dint receive his calls ever again after that. She also blocked him from every single platform. In the 1–2 hours of his flight, she ghosted him completely. He had no idea what happened in that one hour. He tried calling her parents, they din't pick up either. Fast forward 3 months later, she was engaged to someone else. It was a love marriage. She was cheating on him for the past 1 year. All the time when they were apparently happy, he made frequent trips to meet, she talked to his parents often. Since I was their common friend, I had to break the news to him. It was one of the worst calls I ever had to make. I could hear him breaking down. He kept asking if I was kidding. He just couldn't believe she could do this. He simply couldn't understand the reason. I wanted to say “I told you so” but I didn't. She was a serial cheater. He was just another of her recreations. Till her wedding day he kept trying to talk to her just to understand the reason. Of course, she had still blocked him. He went into depression. He started drinking so much that his HOD threatened to suspend him from residency. My best friend who never even drank beer before, spend days drinking and crying and calling her now changed phone number. She on the other hand, continued her merry life, had a lavish wedding and posted a million pictures of her honeymoon. But karma, as they say, is a bi**h. 9 months after her wedding, her husband (the one she cheated on my friend with) cheated on her. She found pictures of him in bed with the other girl on his phone. I actually felt bad for her since she is my friend too, but I couldn't help but see justice in what happened. So if anyone ever hurts you this way, just remember you don't need to dirty your hands. Just sit back and let karma take its course. Because more often than not, it doesn't disappoint.

Question: What made you happy recently?
Answer: This made me very very happy today! By this I mean a version of this in my kitchen! A basket full of fresh, ripe, juicy mangoes! She felt nostalgic, she felt a longing, she felt grief, she felt joy, she felt loved…all in that one moment. It's funny how such small things like a fruit make such an impact. My mother is 60 yrs old now, is a grandmother herself; but in that moment all I could see was a little girl! In that one mango tree, her childhood still survives.

Question: What was the most messed up punishment(s) you received as a child?

Question: What are the weirdest reasons to reject a prospective bride/groom in an arranged marriage?
Answer: This is about my elder sister. She's a lawyer and has completed visharad in music (it's a degree in classical music/dance that you get after 7 long years of practice). Of all the weird reasons I have heard, this seemed really really shallow. I mean, this was 2011 not 1900s! Plot twist - I came across his FB profile a few days back (hence this answer), there was a picture of him, his wife (with apparently a perfect eyesight!) and son. Question: What made you happy today?
Answer: I was sitting in the clinic. It was a very busy OPD. Typical Monday morning rush of patients. The anxiety of a new patient, the comfortable familiarity of some old ones..the usual! That's when he came. He was a fit looking gentleman in his 50s. But with clear signs of being a smoker. Without going into details, he was suffering from an ailment clearly related to smoking. After writing down his prescriptions and some tests, I asked him about his smoking habit. He sheepishly replied. I told him he should cut down, expecting a curt nod (that's what I usually get from habitual smokers). But his reply surprised me, and made me very very happy! Here it goes, Him- yes, infact I have started cutting down a lot since the past 2 weeks. Me- what happened 2 weeks back? Him- my daughter in law gave birth to a baby girl. I always wanted a daughter but we have 2 sons. So this granddaughter is a gift from the heavens. I have promised my DIL that I won't touch the baby till I quit smoking. I am going to see her next month and I have to quit smoking till then! My DIL is like my daughter and how can a father break a promise made to his daughter? I was stunned! In a major part of India, having a daughter is not exactly a reason to celebrate. And here was this guy, not only treating his DIL like a daughter, but going to such lengths (quitting smoking is very, very hard obviously!) for his granddaughter was so heartwarming! I felt just so damn happy! It's things like this that make me hopeful!

Question: What are some funny stories from your college days?
Answer: College days! It hasn't been that long and it already seems a lifetime ago! I studied in Mumbai. Seth GS Medical College! I lived in a hostel. I had my girl gang to hang out with. We lived together, studied together, went out together. And it was just so much fun! Outside the hospital, we were just a bunch of silly 19–20 year olds enjoying aamchi Mumbai! So on one of those outing me and my 4 girl friends went to Colaba. It has a huge Street market. So after wasting an unjustified amount of money and energy on buying things we definitely didn't need, we went to Theobroma. It is a kind of a dessert and chocolate shop. Its pretty famous and pretty old. It is most famous for its chocolate brownies and rum chocolates. Its display usually looks like this (Image source- Google) (I am already drooling!) So as we were sitting there, gossiping and eating brownies my friend, who knew I don't drink, dared me to eat a dozen rum chocolates. I had never even had a beer, let alone rum, but I went ahead anyway. So I ordered a box of rum chocolates and took a teeny tiny bite. As yummy as it was, it had a strong punch of rum. I kept eating till the very last one. Now, they are in no way strong enough to actually make you drunk but I guess it had more of a psychological effect on me. Or maybe it did affect me since I don't drink. But in any case, I felt drunk! So when we walked back to the local station I was slightly tipsy. We got in the train, next stop was Marine drive. I suddenly had the crazy idea to get down and go to the beach. Ofcourse none of my friends agreed since it was already 10 and my hostel had a curfew of 11. As we debated, the train started moving. Without even thinking I jumped out of the train. And BAAAMMMM. I fell face flat on a crowded Marine lines station. A small crowd gathered around me, as I regained my senses I looked around and asked, “Where are my shopping bags!?” I could hear people laughing at me. Who thinks of shopping bags on waking up from a fall?? Me, that's who! The train was super slow, so I wasn't hurt but I was super embarrassed. I narrated this whole scene the next morning, and was ridiculed for weeks for getting drunk on rum chocolates! P. S. Jumping from or getting in moving trains is incredibly reckless and highly dangerous. Please do not, ever, try it. I was lucky to get out unscratched. Not everyone comes out with a laugh.

Question: What’s the worst way you've been woken up?
Answer: I was sleeping in my room. My phone rang around 6.45, it was my dad calling. I din't find it wierd since he calls sometime to wake me up or if he needs a ride. I picked up half asleep. He said, “Kailas mama(uncle) expired.” I couldn't think, I froze, maybe I screamed, it's very hard to remember. I asked him the same question 3 times. He repeated the same thing. I felt numb. My uncle was someone I always looked upto. He wasn't just an uncle, he was an inspiration for me. I took great pride in telling people I am his niece. He was a part of my identity. He was very a successful person. And was famous for his generosity. He was a self made man. And what a man he was! He had reached great heights and yet he was just as humble. He was a MLA and yet his door and his heart was open to everyone, big and small. To his family, to us ,he as pillar supporting us all. I couldn't understand if it's a nightmare or reality. I so desperately wanted it to be a dream, I went back to sleep. Hoping it'll somehow change. It didn't. I woke up, cried my eyes out. Went to the hospital. I went to see him, but I came back from his room. I just couldn't do it. He was not old, it was just too unexpected. It was more shocking because to me he was a hero. And sometimes, you think heroes are immortal. They're not. That is the worst way that I have woken up. Life was never the same after that. There's a big vacuum ever since we lost him. If only that morning was different.

Name: Siya Patil
Question: What does it feel like to get over someone?
Answer: Liberating! I broke up with my boyfriend after 4 years. Actually I din't even break up, neither did he, we simply dissolved somehow. And I think that's the worst, there was no big fight, no cheating, we just drifted apart. And for years after that I kept looking for reasons. He abandoned me when I needed him the most. And even then I refused to give up. I kept trying to mend things, trying to give in to every one of his unreasonable demands but no avail. He was long gone. The phone calls went from thrice a day to once a month and then not even that. Missed birthdays, anniversary, valentine's… He abandoned me, us. But refused to break up. He din't want the blame you see, so he chose to torture me till I do the ugly task. It was so so hard. I used to cry myself to sleep most nights, I started gaining weight, lost interest in friends, going out, shopping. There came a point when I couldn't sleep without taking sleeping pills, and sometimes even those din't help. I just din't know what to do with life. I knew I was sinking, and I knew I needed to change this. So I went to US for a few months. The whole new country, atmosphere helped me heal. After a few months there, I called him to tell it was over.I could hear the relief in his voice. A few tears later, I deleted his number. (Not that it helped, it took another year to forget his number!) As I let myself enjoy other things in life, I realised I don't need him to be happy. As hard as it was, today I am happier than ever. I spent a couple of years hating him, now I feel nothing for him… neither love, nor hate. That is what it feels like to get over someone. Indifference. Long after a relationship ends, it still goes on in your heart. It refuses to let go. You keep counting anniversaries that'll never come, you keep laughing at his jokes you remember out of no where, you keep crying silent tears at his old msgs, you keep scrolling past his FB page trying to see if he misses you too. Until one day, out of nowhere you realise you forgot his number, seeing his photos doesn't flutter your heart anymore, you delete old conversations without a thought, you stop even hating him… you become free. You become liberated. There's a beautiful line I read and loved, “The opposite of love isn't hate. It's apathy.”

Question: What was the most embarrassing moment in front of your parents?
Answer: Oh my..I almost forgot (intentionally?) about this. So here it goes. I am from India. And here on trucks and other public transport alot of times some catchy slogans are written. They are mostly about public education regarding relevant topics like road safety, education and….safe sex. So when I was about 10 years old and very very naive, I was in the car with my dad, his friend and his friend's kids. We were at a signal, right behind a truck. On that truck was written, “Condom kab kab? Yaun sambandh jab jab” (“when to use condoms? Everytime you have sex) So me being 10 year old and very curious…. I read that aloud and asked my dad, “Baba (dad) what does yaun sambandh mean?” A moment of complete silence. “Baba, what does condom mean?” Silence. Then I, clearly not taking the hint, read it again loudly, made both of my friends read that aloud and then laughed really hard cz for some reason I found that whole phrase extremely funny. All this in a closed car with no route of escape! It took me another 5 years to understand why it was so awkward and why my dad refused to answer! I pity my dad that he had to suffer through the most embarrassing car ride ever!

Name: Siya Patil
Question: What is it like to be raised by an Indian father?
Answer: I am a doctor in my 20s. I had a dream a while back…in my dream I had murdered someone, and as scared as I was , even in my dream the only thought that came in my mind was “Dad will take care of this!” This is just an extreme version of reality but, answers the question. This is what it is like being brought up by an Indian father. My father has brought me up in a way that I never really experienced any hardships of life till I moved to a different city for medical school. He has protected me from every possible hardship. He has always, always been there for me. He was there for every elocution competition I was in, he was there when I couldn't clear my entrance in 1st attempt, he was there when I did clear it later on, he is there now when I am in a pretty bad stage in life. Whether this over protective approach is good or bad is up for debate. But for me, I know how much he would have to suffer to give me a life so protected and beautiful. He isn't a typical Indian dad though. He has always encouraged me to go after my dreams, to be independent, to do things just for the sake of it! Even at 27, he hasn't once told me I should get married (to my mother's extreme annoyance!!) Maybe it's because of this level of trust that even after growing up in an over protective family, I managed pretty well to live on my own in Mumbai. As cliche as it may sound, my dad has brought me up like a princess. Love you so much Baba!

Question: Did your mom go to college?
Answer: Yes she did! She got her PhD in protozoology! We belong to a pretty conservative community. And my mom lived in a village. Being the only girl with 5 brothers she was really pampered and over protected. But, she wanted to study.. Every year my grandfather asked her to stop studying, and every year she pleaded for just one more year… this went on from 10th then 12th then BSc then MSc then she started her research for PhD. She got married to my dad after that (He's a doctor..his story is even more inspiring…. That's for some other day!). After her marriage and one kid, my mom completed her PhD while pregnant for the second time. But…my mom's parents were extremely supportive…. When they realised her interest in studies, they moved her to a city. My grandfather went to live in a city for their education while my grandmother stayed back and took care of the farm and house. This was 40yrs back when people din't give that much importance to money. My father also has been incredibly supportive. So is his mom. She took care of all us so that my mom could focus on her career. Now my mother is a professor, highly respected in her field, has been the head speaker in many international conferences, has written 2 books and raised 4 wonderful (I hope we're wonderful!!!) kids….all this from a lil girl in a village!! My God, I am just so very proud of her. If I could someday be even half a woman that my Aai is….i would have achieved my dreams. Bless you a long healthy life ahead Aai…you continue to inspire me every single day.

Name: Siya Patil
Question: What is the most unforgettable sentence that someone said to you?
Answer: I am a doctor. When I was in medical school, there was an old lady admitted for a mass in her liver. She was from my hometown so I used to visit her everyday as I was posted in that same department. She was a very kind old lady and her daughter and son-in-law stayed with her 24*7. Her's was a complicated case since even after days of different tests her condition wasn't diagnosed. After almost 2 weeks, the final results came. She had a very advanced stage intestinal cancer with metastatis in liver. It was so advanced that the consultant advised to take her home for palliative care without any further treatment. She barely had a month to live. They told the facts to her family but she dint know the details (on her own request.) I knew all this. When I went there to bid them goodbye, I was so emotional I could barely speak. Then she said, with all her love and innocence, “next time you come home, I'll definitely come see you”. That was it, I couldn't hold my tears anymore. As optimistic as I am, the doctor in me knew she'll be long gone by then. That was definitely the saddest thing anyone ever said to me. Also, the most unforgettable. More so because the person was too naive to know the harsh reality. That was also the day I realised that truth is indeed overrated.
